questions.prompt: Why does Swift not allow integer subscripting on strings like `text[0]`, and why does it use `String.Index` instead? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that Unicode characters take different byte sizes in UTF-8
Explains that finding the nth character means walking from the start
Notes that Swift uses String.Index to avoid hidden slow O(n) steps

questions.modelAnswer: Swift does not allow integer subscripting on strings because Unicode characters have different byte sizes in UTF-8. One visual character can take 1 byte or many bytes. Finding the nth character means walking from the start of the string, which takes O(n) time. Swift uses String.Index so programmers see this traversal cost clearly.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Strings and Characters

questions.prompt: What is an extended grapheme cluster, and how does canonical equivalence work when comparing strings in Swift? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Defines an extended grapheme cluster as one or more Unicode scalars forming one readable character
Explains that canonical equivalence matches characters with the same visual appearance and meaning
Notes that precomposed and decomposed forms compare as equal with ==

questions.modelAnswer: An extended grapheme cluster is one or more Unicode scalars that join to make one human-readable character. In Swift, string comparison with `==` uses canonical equivalence. Two strings are equal if their grapheme clusters have the same visual look and meaning. For example, a single `é` matches `e` followed by a combining accent mark.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Strings and Characters

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between `String` and `Substring` in Swift. Why should you convert a `Substring` to a `String` before saving it in a long-lived property? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that Substring shares the memory buffer of its parent String
States that keeping a Substring stops the parent buffer from being freed
States that String(substring) creates an independent buffer

questions.modelAnswer: A `Substring` is a slice that shares the memory buffer of its parent `String`, so slicing is fast. However, keeping a `Substring` keeps the whole parent string alive in memory. If you slice a small word from a huge text file, the whole file stays in memory. Converting the slice with `String(substring)` makes a new buffer so the original file can be freed.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Strings and Characters

questions.prompt: How does `endIndex` on a `String` differ from the position of the last character? What happens if you subscript `text[text.endIndex]`? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that endIndex points to the position after the last character
Explains that reading text[text.endIndex] causes a fatal runtime crash
States that the last character is reached with index(before: text.endIndex)

questions.modelAnswer: In Swift, `endIndex` points to the position right after the last character in a string. It marks the end boundary for half-open ranges. Reading `text[text.endIndex]` causes a fatal out-of-bounds crash at runtime. To get the last character of a non-empty string, use `text.index(before: text.endIndex)`.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Strings and Characters

questions.prompt: Explain how Swift strings combine value semantics with good performance using Copy-on-Write (COW). Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that String is a struct with value semantics
Explains that Copy-on-Write shares the memory buffer across copies until a change happens
Notes that this avoids unneeded memory copies when strings are only read

questions.modelAnswer: Swift strings are value types built as structs, so each variable keeps independent text. Behind the scenes, Swift saves memory and time using Copy-on-Write. Multiple string variables share the same memory buffer until one of them changes. Only when a change happens does Swift allocate a new copy, giving both safety and speed.
